name: Cavitation (ultrasonic fat)

image.caption: Principe de récupération d'énergie par cavitation acoustique 2

lead: Ultrasonic cavitation uses low-frequency ultrasound through a handheld probe to target fat under the skin without surgery. It is sold in clinics and as cheap home units, and some looksmaxxing posters use it to slim the face and chin.

The idea is that ultrasound creates bubbles that collapse near cells and damage fat cell membranes, which lab studies of cells and vessels document. A few small human trials are registered, mainly on abdominal fat in women, with no results summarised. Forum users are split between those reporting benefit and those reporting none.

paras: People use home devices as a DIY way to spot-reduce fat on the cheeks and under the chin, while clinics offer it for body areas in a series of sessions.

The sources reviewed do not report adverse events from cosmetic cavitation. Lab studies show cavitation can damage cells and small vessels, and device quality varies widely. Regulatory status varies by device and country.

angle.text: Forum users, especially for DIY face slimming, use cavitation devices hoping to burst fat cells and slim the cheeks, jaw or belly. Only small registered trials exist, and no cosmetic results were located for the home-use claim.

lead: Ultrasonic cavitation, also sold as "lipocavitation", is a non-invasive body-contouring treatment in which a handheld device applies low-frequency ultrasound to the skin over a fat deposit. Marketing and forum guides say the sound waves form tiny bubbles in the tissue that burst and break open fat cells, after which the body clears the contents.[1]

Cavitation itself, the formation and collapse of gas bubbles in a liquid under ultrasound, is a well-studied physical phenomenon, and laboratory work has examined how inertial cavitation affects cells and blood vessels in vitro.[2][3][4] Whether consumer or spa devices reproduce these effects in living subcutaneous fat at a cosmetically visible scale is a separate question; the sources reviewed here include a handful of small registered clinical trials, mostly of abdominal fat in women, with no published results summarised in the registry entries.[5][6]

In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed mainly as an at-home method for "spot reducing" facial and submental fat using inexpensive devices. Some users report improvements; others describe it as ineffective.[1][7]

Abdomen, thighs, flanks; at home, face and chin
Limited: lab studies of cavitation, small registered clinical trials

paras: Cavitation devices apply low-frequency ultrasound through a coupling gel with a moving probe. Clinic machines and cheaper consumer units both carry the "cavitation" label and differ widely in power and design; the sources reviewed do not give standardised specifications for either.
Forum users often describe combining a cavitation unit with radiofrequency.[7]

In physics, acoustic cavitation refers to bubbles that grow and collapse under alternating pressure. Reviews describe that collapse (inertial cavitation) as capable of mechanical, thermal and chemical effects on nearby cells, including transient membrane permeabilisation known as sonoporation.[2][3] Microscopy work has shown cavitating microbubbles can deform small blood vessels on microsecond timescales.[4] These studies used cell cultures or specialised experimental setups, often with microbubble agents, and are not trials of cosmetic fat reduction.

Proponents of the cosmetic use say the effect selectively ruptures adipocytes and that released lipid is cleared by the lymphatic system and liver.[1] No study among those reviewed directly demonstrates this sequence in people treated with cosmetic devices.

A small number of human trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. They include a comparison of cavitation frequencies on abdominal adiposity in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (30 participants, completed),[5] a phase 2 trial of cavitation ultrasound in PCOS with 198 participants (completed),[6] a trial of cavitation versus electrolipolysis in obese infertile women with PCOS,[8] a trial in adolescent females with abdominal obesity,[9] and a trial of insulin resistance in women with central obesity that was recruiting at last listing.[10] Other registrations cover lipedema and postnatal women with diastasis recti.[11][12]

These registrations list conditions such as obesity or PCOS rather than cosmetic facial contouring, and the registry entries do not report outcome results. No registered trial in these sources studies at-home facial cavitation devices.

A long looksmax.org guide presents ultrasonic cavitation as a way to reduce subcutaneous facial fat at home; its author notes that other users often dismiss the method, and the post carries a disclaimer that it is not medical advice.[1] In another thread a user starting cavitation with radiofrequency says it should work, a replying user says they tried it and recommends an injectable fat-dissolving product instead, and the original poster answers that the failed attempt may have involved a poor device.[7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, cavitation is discussed as a cheap, non-surgical facial slimming option, with posters split between those who report benefit and those who say it fails.[1][7]
